description_full: Extreme Networks, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, develops, markets, and sells network infrastructure equipment and related software in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia-Pacific. It offers ExtremeCloud IQ, a machine learning/AI powered, wired and wireless cloud network management solution that offers visibility and control over users, devices, and applications; ExtremeCloud IQ-Site Engine which extends cloud management to non-cloud native and multi-vendor devices; ExtremeCloud IQ Essentials provides wireless intrusion prevention system, location services, and guest management services; and ExtremeCloud SD-WAN, a software-defined wide area networks solution offered as an all-inclusive subscription, which includes hardware, the cloud-based SD-WAN service, support and maintenance, and customer success support. The company also provides indoor and outdoor Wi-Fi 7 and prior generation Aps; WIPS solutions; switch products; Cloud Native Platforms and Applications for Service Providers; and ExtremeCloud Universal ZTNA. In addition, the company offers customer and support services, such as support services for end-users, resellers, and distributors; and premier, professional, and education services. It sells its products through original equipment manufacturers, strategic relationships, distributors, resellers, and field sales. The company serves mid-market and enterprise customers, and services providers. Extreme Networks, Inc., was incorporated in 1996 and is headquartered in Morrisville, North Carolina.

financial_summary: Extreme Networks, Inc. is a mid-cap technology business with a $3.2B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 25% against a 10% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 55% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $95M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.92× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 4.5×.

Shareholder yield of 2.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 3.1% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 5% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.21x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-5.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 40% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 13% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 29% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 54% and a beta of 1.20, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.59 vs 5y 1.34), so read it loosely.
About $32.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 76% in the 2020 crash, 45% in the 2022 bear market and 70% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $10.47 (margin of safety -130%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 59%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $6.11 to $18.08 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 61.6 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 27.0 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 33.1 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 8 covering analysts target $33.62 on average, 40% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 25% clears the cost of capital of 10.5% by 14pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 13.65).
It runs a 55% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow, or 1% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 2.92x.
ROE of 48% is amplified by 13.3x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 18.2% of revenue on R&D and 6.9% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $48.0M (2% of market cap).
The current ratio of 0.93 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -0.7% over 3 years, 4.9% over 5 years and 9.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 25%).
At current returns, reinvesting 43% of profits supports about 10.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -5.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.03, a backlog worth 51% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 6%.
Capex runs 1.8x depreciation (2.2% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 5, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.1%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (10 sales, net $9.2M sold).
It returns 2.8% a year to shareholders (2.8% in buybacks).
people: With about 2,894 employees, each generates about $444K of revenue, 1.2x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 10.4% a year.
That works out to $33K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.9M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
